Based on Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (AAPL_2024_10K.pdf), the MD&A discloses four reported results for fiscal 2024 (vs. 2023) that were unfavorably affected by weakness of foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar:

**1. Greater China segment net sales (p. 25, Item 7 "Segment Operating Performance")**
- Greater China net sales decreased 8% to $66,952M from $72,559M, due primarily to lower iPhone and iPad net sales.
- "The weakness in the renminbi relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Greater China net sales during 2024."

**2. Japan segment net sales (p. 25)**
- Japan net sales increased 3% to $25,052M from $24,257M, due primarily to higher iPhone net sales.
- "The weakness in the yen relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Japan net sales during 2024."

**3. Rest of Asia Pacific segment net sales (p. 25)**
- Rest of Asia Pacific net sales increased 4% to $30,658M from $29,615M, due primarily to higher Services net sales.
- "The weakness of foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar had a net unfavorable year-over-year impact on Rest of Asia Pacific net sales during 2024."

**4. Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage (p. 27)**
- Products gross margin rose to $109,633M (37.2%) from $108,803M (36.5%), but "the increase in Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage ... [was] partially offset by a different Products mix and the weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar."

- This $58 million represents the portion of dividends accrued from the October 31, 2024 issuance date through December 31, 2024 (i.e., the accumulated stub-period dividends), as distinct from the $72 million first full quarterly dividend declared in December 2024 and paid in January 2025.

**3. $345 million — the expected annual cash dividend requirement (a forward-looking figure, not a 2024 charge)**
- Item 1A, "Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity" (p. 17): "we expect to require up to $345 million of cash per year for the payment of dividends on the outstanding shares of our 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock ... through the mandatory conversion date of October 15, 2027."

| Amount | Meaning | Where disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| $72 million | First quarterly dividend declared (Dec 2024, record date Jan 1, 2025; $12.50/share); paid in cash Jan 15, 2025 | Note 19, p. 106; Statements of Equity, p. 58 |
| $58 million | Dividends accumulated during 2024 (from the Oct 31, 2024 issuance through Dec 31, 2024), deducted in arriving at net loss attributable to common shareholders and in the EPS computation | Statements of Operations p. 54; Note 4, p. 73 |
| $345 million | Expected annual cash needed for preferred dividends through mandatory conversion on October 15, 2027 (forward-looking liquidity requirement) | Item 1A Risk Factors, p. 17 |

## Answer (JPMorgan Chase & Co. 2023 Form 10-K)

The Firm adopted the new TDR guidance (ASC 326‑20‑30‑3A, "Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings") on January 1, 2023 under the **modified retrospective method**. Two amounts are disclosed:

### 1. Allowance for credit losses / allowance for loan losses: $(587) million (a net decrease)
Disclosed in Note 1 (p. 173 of the 10‑K) and Note 13 (p. 256): the adoption "resulted in a net decrease to the allowance for credit losses of **$587 million**."

In the Note 13 allowance rollforward, this appears as the line "Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle" (footnote: impact to the allowance for loan losses upon adoption of the TDR guidance), by portfolio segment (in millions):

| Portfolio segment | Effect on allowance for loan losses |
|---|---|
| Consumer, excluding credit card | $(489) |
| Credit card | $(100) |
| Wholesale | $2 |
| **Total** | **$(587)** |

- Allowance for lending-related commitments: **no effect** (shown as "NA").
- Allowance for credit losses on investment securities: **no effect**.

**What it measures:** the reduction in the credit-loss allowance caused by the accounting change itself — eliminating TDR accounting/disclosure (including the requirement to measure the allowance using a discounted cash flow method) and electing the Firm's **non‑DCF, portfolio‑based** allowance approach for loans modified for borrowers in financial difficulty (in all portfolios except collateral‑dependent loans and nonaccrual risk‑rated loans, for which the asset‑specific DCF approach continues, now using the post‑modification effective interest rate). The reduction was "predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card." Note 13 also states the allowance for credit losses "reflected a reduction of $587 million as a result of the adoption of changes to the TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023."

### 2. Retained earnings: $446 million (an increase, after tax)
Note 1 and Note 13: the adoption resulted in "an increase to retained earnings of **$446 million, after‑tax**" — the tax-effected counterpart of the $587 million pretax allowance reduction.

The Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity shows a 2023 line "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" of **$449 million** added to retained earnings; that total covers the TDR adoption ($446 million) plus the concurrently adopted portfolio‑layer fair‑value hedge accounting guidance, whose retained‑earnings impact the Firm describes as immaterial.

**What it measures:** the after‑tax cumulative‑effect adjustment to shareholders' equity (opening retained earnings) resulting from the change in accounting principle — i.e., the $587 million pretax allowance reduction net of the related tax benefit.

### Other context
- No amounts are disclosed for the TDR adoption at the **business‑segment** level (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM); the only segment-level detail is by credit portfolio segment (consumer ex‑card, credit card, wholesale) shown above.
- The adoption also eliminated TDR disclosures and introduced "financial difficulty modifications" (FDM) disclosure; 2023 FDMs were $136 million for residential real estate, $648 million for credit card, and $2.1 billion for wholesale, versus 2022 TDRs of $362 million, $418 million, and $801 million, respectively.

## NVIDIA FY2024 Form 10‑K (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024) — inventory provisions and related releases charged to cost of revenue

**Document:** NVDA_2024_10K.pdf (Item 7 MD&A, Note 1, Note 10, and the PwC Critical Audit Matter)

### 1. Total gross provisions charged to cost of revenue — $2.2 billion
MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" (Item 7):
> "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled **$2.2 billion** for both fiscal years 2024 and 2023. Sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations resulted in a provision release of **$540 million** ... for fiscal years 2024 and 2023, respectively."

The $2.2 billion is disclosed in two components elsewhere in the filing (Note 10), which together reconcile to it:

### 2. Component A — inventory write-down: $774 million
Note 10, footnote (1) to the Inventories table (raw materials $1,719M; work-in-process $1,505M; finished goods $2,058M; total $5,282M):
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an inventory provision of **$774 million** and $1.0 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue."

This is the write-down of inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value for excess or obsolete inventory (per Note 1: "Most of our inventory provisions relate to excess quantities of products, based on our inventory levels and future product purchase commitments compared to assumptions about future demand and market conditions").

### 3. Component B — excess purchase obligations: approximately $1.4 billion
Note 10, footnote (1) to the "Accrued and Other Current Liabilities" table (the line item "Excess inventory purchase obligations" of $1,655M at year-end, which is a balance and therefore excluded per your instruction):
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an expense of approximately **$1.4 billion** and $1.1 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue for **inventory purchase obligations in excess of our current demand projections, supplier charges and for penalties related to cancellations and underutilization**."

So Component B covers three things: purchase commitments in excess of demand projections, supplier charges, and cancellation/underutilization penalties.

### 4. Provision release: $540 million
As above, in fiscal 2024 NVIDIA recorded a **$540 million release** of cost of revenue, arising from (a) sales of previously reserved inventory and/or (b) settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations. The filing does not break the $540 million down between these two sources. (Note 1 confirms that once inventory is written down it "creates a new cost basis for the inventory that is not subsequently written-up," so a release can also come from settlement of the corresponding purchase-commitment liability.)

### 5. Net fiscal 2024 effect
Gross provisions of $2.2 billion ($774M + ~$1.4B) less the $540 million release = a **net charge to cost of revenue of approximately $1.6 billion** in fiscal 2024.

### Related but distinct items (for clarity, not part of the above)
- $33 million cost-of-revenue benefit from the February 2023 change in useful lives of property and equipment (accounting-estimate change; also produced a $102M operating-expense benefit, $135M operating income and $114M net income benefit) — not an inventory provision.
- The $2.5 billion of short-term prepaid supply and capacity agreements and $16.1 billion of outstanding inventory purchase and long-term supply/capacity obligations (Note 13) are year-end balances, excluded per your instruction, though the PwC Critical Audit Matter ("Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments") references them as the basis for the significant judgment in these estimates.

## Walmart FY2022 Form 10-K (FY ended January 31, 2022) — pickup and delivery location counts

The filing gives these counts in three places, each tied to a different scope of the business:

**1. Company-wide / global (Item 1, "The Development of Our Company")**
- "To date, we now have **over 8,000 pickup and 6,000 delivery locations globally**."
- Scope: the entire company globally (all segments), in the historical narrative of the company's eCommerce/omni-channel development. The pickup qualifier is "over"; the delivery figure is stated plainly as "6,000" (no "over"/"approximately" qualifier on the delivery number itself).

**2. Walmart U.S. segment (Item 1, "Walmart U.S. Segment" — Omni-channel)**
- "As of January 31, 2022, we had **approximately 4,600 pickup locations and more than 3,500 same-day delivery locations**."
- Scope: the Walmart U.S. segment (Walmart and Neighborhood Market brands in the 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico), covering the pickup and **same-day delivery** services of its omni-channel offering (alongside ship-from-store, digital pharmacy fulfillment, Walmart+).

**3. Walmart International segment (Item 1, "Walmart International Segment" — Omni-channel)**
- "As of January 31, 2022, Walmart International had **approximately 2,900 pickup and over 1,900 delivery locations**."
- Scope: the Walmart International segment (23 countries outside the U.S. as of January 31, 2022), covering its pickup and delivery services, including same-day delivery expansion in Mexico, the one-hour delivery partnerships with JD.com/JD Daojia in China, and Flipkart/PhonePe in India.

**Notes on scope and exclusions**
- These are the only pickup/delivery location counts in the filing. Sam's Club's segment description gives no pickup or delivery location count (it only describes Curbside Pickup at all clubs, delivery-from-club and ship-from-club).
- The counts should not be confused with the network infrastructure figures the filing separately reports, which are explicitly distribution, fulfillment or sort facilities: Walmart U.S. — 157 distribution facilities, 31 dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers, and shipping/delivery from "more than 3,500 stores"; Walmart International — 179 distribution facilities, 83 dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers, and "more than 3,400 eCommerce sort centers and last-mile delivery facilities in India"; Sam's Club — 28 dedicated distribution facilities and 12 dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers.
- The segment counts (approx. 4,600 + approx. 2,900 pickup; more than 3,500 + over 1,900 delivery) do not sum exactly to the global "over 8,000 pickup and 6,000 delivery locations" figure, reflecting rounding and the different as-of framing (global statement is "to date"; segment statements are as of January 31, 2022).

## NVIDIA FY2025 Form 10-K — Factors Affecting Gross Margin

**Headline:** Gross margin rose to 75.0% in fiscal 2025 from 72.7% in fiscal 2024 (cost of revenue fell from 27.3% to 25.0% of revenue).

### Favorable factors

**1. Higher mix of Data Center revenue — the primary driver.** Both the "Fiscal Year 2025 Summary" and the "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" section in Item 7 MD&A state that gross margin increased "primarily driven by a higher mix of Data Center revenue." Data Center revenue grew 142% in fiscal 2025 (driven by demand for the Hopper platform for large language models, recommendation engines and generative AI), with Data Center computing revenue up 162%, while Compute & Networking segment revenue rose 145% to $116.2 billion. Because Data Center products carry structurally higher gross margins than the Gaming, Professional Visualization and Automotive businesses, the shift in revenue mix toward Data Center was the key favorable factor. (Gaming grew9%, Professional Visualization 21%, and Automotive 55%.)

**2. A smaller year-over-year inventory drag.** The net effect of inventory provisions and sales of previously reserved inventory was an unfavorable impact of 2.3% on gross margin in fiscal 2025, versus 2.7% in fiscal 2024. So although inventory remained a headwind, the drag was roughly 0.4 points smaller than in the prior year, contributing favorably to the year-over-year change.

**3. A smaller unfavorable effect from provision releases on a comparative basis.** Sales of previously reserved inventory and settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations produced provision releases of $689 million in fiscal 2025 versus $540 million in fiscal 2024 — a modestly larger favorable offset.

**4. Slightly lower acquisition-related intangible amortization.** Amortization expense on amortizable intangibles declined to $593 million in fiscal 2025 from $614 million in fiscal 2024 (and $699 million in fiscal 2023), a modest favorable item within cost of revenue.

### Unfavorable factors

**1. Inventory provisions and excess inventory purchase obligations — the principal unfavorable factor.** Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $3.7 billion in fiscal 2025, versus $2.2 billion in fiscal 2024. These consist of (a) an inventory provision of $1.6 billion recorded in cost of revenue in fiscal 2025 (versus $774 million in fiscal 2024), and (b) approximately $2.0 billion of expense in cost of revenue related to excess inventory purchase obligations (versus $1.4 billion in fiscal 2024). The net effect of provisions net of releases was an unfavorable 2.3% impact on gross margin in fiscal 2025 (2.7% in fiscal 2024). The ending reserve for excess inventory purchase obligations was $2.1 billion, and the accrued product warranty and return provisions balance rose to $1.373 billion from $415 million.

**2. Product transitions driving excess/obsolete inventory.** Under Critical Accounting Estimates, NVIDIA identifies the drivers of excess or obsolete inventory and excess purchase commitments as including "new product introductions resulting in less demand for existing products," changes in market and economic conditions, sudden decreases in demand, inventory obsolescence from changing technology and customer requirements, and failure to estimate demand properly. This is directly relevant given the annual product cadence in fiscal 2025 — the Hopper architecture drove demand for the full year, while production shipments of the Blackwell architecture only began in the fourth quarter — and the resulting overlap of prior- and next-generation architectures in the supply chain.

**3. Long manufacturing lead times and non-cancellable capacity commitments.** NVIDIA notes that manufacturing lead times "can be and have been long, and in some cases, extended beyond twelve months for some products," and that it places non-cancellable inventory orders in advance of historical lead times, "pay[s] premiums and provide[s] deposits to secure future supply and capacity." These practices carry cost that flows through cost of revenue and contributed to the elevated purchase commitments and provisions.

**4. Macroeconomic and cost pressures within cost of revenue.** In the MD&A Overview, NVIDIA notes that macroeconomic factors — inflation, interest rate changes, capital market volatility, global supply chain constraints, and tariffs — "impact our supply chain and manufacturing costs, employee wages, costs for capital equipment and value of our investments," while adding that "our product and solution pricing generally does not fluctuate with short-term changes in our costs." Cost of revenue also includes memory and component costs, board and device costs, manufacturing support costs, final test yield fallout, tariffs, and shipping costs, all of which bear on gross margin.

## Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K — causes of lower commercial airplane (BCA) deliveries in 2024

**The fact pattern:** Boeing's BCA delivered **348 airplanes in 2024 vs. 528 in 2023** (2024: 737 = 265, 747 = 0, 767 = 18, 777 = 14, 787 = 51; 2023: 737 = 396, 747 = 1, 767 = 32, 777 = 26, 787 = 73). MD&A states BCA revenues fell because of "lower deliveries across all programs and 737-9 customer considerations related to the January 2024 grounding," and the cash-flow discussion attributes lower deliveries to safety/quality actions, supply chain constraints and the IAM 751 work stoppage.

### Causes the filing explicitly links to deliveries (five distinct drivers)

**1. The Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident and the FAA's resulting regulatory response (January 2024).**
The filing says the accident "significantly impacted" 2024 results; the FAA grounded ~220 737-9s, all 737-9s in production had to undergo an enhanced inspection process *prior to delivery*, the FAA investigated the 737 quality control system (including Spirit), and the FAA "will not approve production rate increases beyond 38 per month or additional production lines until Boeing has complied with required quality and safety standards." Boeing slowed rates, delayed planned rate increases and added Spirit fuselage inspections — directly reducing 737 output and deliveries.

**2. The IAM 751 work stoppage (September 13 – November 4, 2024).**
Production of 737, 767, 777 and 777X (plus some BDS derivatives) was paused; production resumed only in December 2024. The filing states plainly: "The IAM 751 work stoppage significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024."

**3. Supply chain constraints and supplier quality/performance disruptions.**
787 production was slowed to below 5 per month "due to supply chain constraints as well as other production issues"; 767 experienced "factory disruption, including supply chain delays and quality issues," slowing production, which resumed only in December. These supply disruptions and the resulting inventory build (commercial aircraft program inventories rose from $68.7B to $75.2B; "growth in Inventories was primarily driven by lower deliveries") are tied to the delivery shortfall.

**4. Delayed FAA certification of new and derivative models, which pushed deliveries out.**
- *737-7 and 737-10:* certification delayed pending an engine anti-ice engineering solution, leaving ~35 aircraft in inventory undelivered at year-end.
- *777X:* flight-test delays and revised certification timelines pushed first 777-9 delivery to 2026, the 777-8 Freighter to 2028, and the 777-8 passenger aircraft to no earlier than 2030; Boeing also slowed the 777X ramp "which resulted in ... further customer delivery delays."

**5. The 787 business class seat delays.**
"Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025."

*(Minor supporting items: the last 747 was delivered in February 2023 and none in 2024; ~55 pre-2023-built 737-8s, including ~40 for China customers, sat in inventory for 2025 delivery.)*

### Causes deliberately excluded (cost/production-rate/revenue only, not delivery-linked)
- **777X and 767 reach-forward losses** of $4,079M (777X $3,499M; 767 $580M) — a loss/charge, not a delivery cause.
- **Abnormal production costs** ($256M on 787 in 2024; the $1,271M year-over-year *decrease* in abnormal production costs) — a cost item.
- **The IAM 751 new agreement and pay increases** (raised 777X/767 costs) — a cost item; only the *strike itself* is linked to deliveries.
- **737-9 customer considerations ($443M charge) and 737 MAX concessions** — revenue/liability items.
- **Higher R&D, supply chain inflation, and BDS fixed-price program losses (T-7A, KC-46A, etc.)** — costs outside BCA deliveries.

**Bottom line:** The 10-K ties the 2024 delivery decline (348 vs. 528) to five delivery-linked causes: the Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident and FAA grounding/oversight/rate cap, the IAM 751 strike, supply chain and supplier quality disruptions, certification delays for the 737-7/-10 and 777X, and 787 business class seat delays — with the earnings charges, cost increases and rate actions that also flowed from these events counted separately as cost/revenue consequences.
